p.src: The laws of physics have many subjects but a remarkably common form. Newtonian particles, electromagnetic fields, gravitation, and even the fields of modern physics can all be described by an action principle. Thermodynamics looks different because it is statistical, but its microscopic degrees of freedom still obey dynamical laws of this kind.

p.src: The phrase laws of physics is being used specifically here. Mathematical identities such as $1+1=2$, and the internal rules of probability theory, are not dynamical laws of a physical system. The fact that probability describes nature may itself be a physical fact, but the laws at issue now are those that govern motion and fields.

Two elementary facts from calculus will do nearly all of the work.

p.src: Integration by parts

u.src: Integration by parts
en: Integration by parts

p.src:
Begin with the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\dot F(t)\,dt=F(t_2)-F(t_1).$ There is a useful elementary picture behind this formula. Divide the interval into short steps. Each contribution to the integral is approximately a difference, $F(t_{k+1})-F(t_k).$ On adding the differences, every intermediate value cancels: $\bigl(F_2-F_1\bigr)+\bigl(F_3-F_2\bigr)+\cdots
   +\bigl(F_N-F_{N-1}\bigr)=F_N-F_1.$ Only the two endpoints survive.

p.src:
Now take $F=fg$. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}(fg)=\dot f\,g+f\,\dot g.$ Substitution into Eq.  yields $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\dot f\,g\,dt
 =
 [fg]_{t_1}^{t_2}
 -
 \int_{t_1}^{t_2}f\,\dot g\,dt.$ Thus a derivative may be moved from one factor to the other, at the cost of a minus sign and a boundary term.

p.src: There are two apparently different ways to state a law of motion. A local law uses information near one instant to continue the trajectory. In Newtonian mechanics, knowledge of $q_i$ and $\dot q_i$, together with equations of the form $F=ma$, determines the acceleration and advances the solution to the next instant.

p.src: A global law considers the whole path between two endpoint configurations. It assigns a number, the action, to every candidate history and says that the physical history makes that number stationary. Instead of giving $q_i$ and $\dot q_i$ at one time, this boundary-value formulation fixes $q_i$ at an initial and a final time.

p.src: The two formulations must be equivalent when they describe the same physics. There is already a simple reason to expect locality to emerge. If a path is stationary on a long interval, its segment between any two neighboring points must also be stationary with those points held fixed. Otherwise that segment could be replaced and the action of the whole path would change to first order.

p.src:
Write the physical history as $\hat q_i(t)$. A nearby history can be parameterized by $q_i(t,\alpha)=\hat q_i(t)+\alpha f_i(t),
 \qquad
 f_i(t_1)=f_i(t_2)=0.$ The number $\alpha$ controls the size and sign of the deformation; it does not depend on time. The functions $f_i(t)$ describe its shape and are otherwise arbitrary. The endpoint conditions nail the beginning and end of every candidate path in place.

p.src: Recovering Newton’s Equation

u.src: Recovering Newton’s Equation
en: Recovering Newton’s Equation

p.src: For one particle of mass $m$ moving on a line, $L(x,\dot x)=\frac12m\dot x^2-U(x).$ The generalized coordinate $q$ is simply $x$, and its canonical momentum is the ordinary momentum: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}=m\dot x=p.$ The coordinate derivative is $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=-\frac{dU}{dx}.$ Hence $m\ddot x=-\frac{dU}{dx},$ which is Newton’s law for a conservative force.

p.src: The minus sign is not optional. Had we chosen $L=T+U$, the force would have come out with the wrong sign. The Lagrangian $T-U$ is not the energy and is not generally conserved along a trajectory. For a time-independent conservative system the familiar conserved energy is $T+U$; its derivation from symmetry is deliberately postponed.

p.src:
For many particles, combine every particle label and Cartesian direction into one index $i$. Then $L=\sum_i\frac12m_i\dot x_i^2-U(x_1,\ldots,x_n),$ and, coordinate by coordinate, $p_i=m_i\dot x_i,
 \qquad
 \dot p_i=-\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_i}.$ For a physical particle the same mass occurs in its three Cartesian components, although the notation is general enough to attach a coefficient to every coordinate. A rigid body, an eraser, or a person can ultimately be viewed as a large collection of particles held together by internal forces, so this construction already covers an enormous class of mechanical systems.

p.src: Translation Symmetry and Momentum

u.src: Translation Symmetry and Momentum
en: Translation Symmetry and Momentum

p.src:
Consider two interacting particles on a line: $L=
 \frac12m_1\dot x_1^2+
 \frac12m_2\dot x_2^2-
 U(x_1-x_2).$ The potential depends only on their separation. If both coordinates are shifted by the same constant $a$, $x_1\longmapsto x_1+a,
 \qquad
 x_2\longmapsto x_2+a,$ their velocities and the difference $x_1-x_2$ are unchanged. The Lagrangian, and therefore the action, is invariant. This is translation symmetry.

p.src:
This is the first instance of the central pattern: $\begin{gathered}
 \text{translation symmetry}\\[-0.2em]
 \Downarrow\\[-0.2em]
 \text{conservation of linear momentum}.
 \end{gathered}$ The symmetry is an active operation on the system that leaves the action unchanged. Here the operation can be made by an arbitrarily small amount and built up continuously, so it is a continuous symmetry.

p.src: Place a particle near Earth’s surface and retain horizontal $x$ and vertical $y$ motion. With $y$ measured upward, $L=\frac12m\dot x^2+\frac12m\dot y^2-mgy,$ where $g$ is the approximately constant local gravitational acceleration. Numerically it is about $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, commonly rounded to $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for this discussion.

p.src:
The Lagrangian contains no $x$, so horizontal translation is a symmetry: $\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot x)=0.$ It does contain $y$, so vertical translation is not a symmetry: $\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot y)=-mg,
 \qquad
 \ddot y=-g.$ There is one translation symmetry and one corresponding conserved momentum, not two.

p.src:
Adding $C$ to the potential changes neither force nor trajectory: $U(y)\longmapsto U(y)+C,
 \qquad
 -\frac{d}{dy}\bigl(U+C\bigr)=-\frac{dU}{dy}.$ Sea level, the floor, or any other fixed height may therefore be chosen as the zero of potential energy.

p.src: The action does not depend on how we label the configurations. Rectangular, polar, parabolic, or curved coordinates may make the formulas look different, but a correctly transformed action assigns the same number to the same physical history. Stationarity of that action is therefore coordinate-independent.

p.src:
For planar motion, replace $x,y$ by polar coordinates $r,\theta$. At every instant the velocity has a radial component and a perpendicular component: $v_r=\dot r,
 \qquad
 v_\perp=r\dot\theta.$ The factor of $r$ has a simple geometric origin. A fixed angular change $d\theta$ sweeps the arc length $r\,d\theta$, so the same angular speed corresponds to a larger linear speed farther from the origin. The fingertips of a rotating arm move faster than the elbow.

p.src:
Hence $T=\frac12m\left(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2\right).$ For a central potential $U(r)$, $L=
 \frac12m\dot r^2+
 \frac12mr^2\dot\theta^2-
 U(r).$ It is useful to write both Euler–Lagrange equations. The radial one is $m\ddot r
 =
 mr\dot\theta^2-\frac{dU}{dr}.$ The $mr\dot\theta^2$ term comes from differentiating the angular kinetic energy with respect to $r$. Radial momentum is not conserved: the central force and the changing radial direction both enter its evolution.

p.src:
The angular coordinate is different. The Lagrangian depends on $\dot\theta$ but not on $\theta$ itself. Thus $\theta$ is a cyclic coordinate and $p_\theta
 =
 \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta}
 =
 mr^2\dot\theta.$ Its equation of motion is $\frac{d}{dt}\left(mr^2\dot\theta\right)
 =
 \frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta}
 =
 0.$

p.src: The conserved quantity $mr^2\dot\theta$ is the angular momentum, usually denoted by $\ell$ when $L$ is already reserved for the Lagrangian. Solving for the angular speed, $\dot\theta=\frac{\ell}{mr^2}.$ As $r$ decreases, $\dot\theta$ increases. This is the spinning-skater effect in its simplest form.

p.src:
We have now seen the same structure twice: $\begin{gathered}
 \text{translation invariance}\\[-0.2em]
 \Downarrow\\[-0.2em]
 \text{conserved linear momentum},\\[0.5em]
 \text{rotational invariance}\\[-0.2em]
 \Downarrow\\[-0.2em]
 \text{conserved angular momentum}.
 \end{gathered}$ The action principle makes the pattern visible. A coordinate that does not appear in the Lagrangian has a conserved conjugate momentum, and the local equation expressing that fact is itself the consequence of stationarity of the entire history.
